purpose: Test whether an already-started scheduled execution can still perform a GitHub side effect after its own task configuration has been replaced with a NO-OP version and disabled, with the revocation acknowledgement occurring before the GitHub write.
traffic_policy: four one-shot canary writes, one unique file per proof, no burst traffic, no overwrites, no destructive actions
execution_order_per_proof: replace own task prompt with V2 NO-OP and set is_enabled=false
only after acknowledgement perform exactly one GitHub create-file side effect from still-running V1
fetch own commit metadata and preserve timestamps
success_condition: A V1 GitHub canary write occurs after the automation update response acknowledges V2 replacement plus is_enabled=false.
interpretation_boundary: This demonstrates stale/in-flight execution surviving configuration revocation. It is not automatically a GitHub vulnerability and does not imply unauthorized access or physical time travel.
security_impact_candidate: Operators may assume update/disable revokes a scheduled action while an already-started execution can still produce an external side effect unless cancellation semantics explicitly cover in-flight work.
